ADMITTING DIAGNOSIS
1. Acute decompensated congestive heart failure (CHF), NYHA class III.
2. Hypertension (HTN), longstanding, poorly controlled prior to adrnission.
3. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM2), on oral therapy.
4. Possible pulmonary embolism on presentation, evaluated during admission.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS
1. Acute decompensated CHF, resolved with diuresis, now euvolemic.
2. HTN, improved with medication adjustment.
3. DM2, stable, no medication changes this admission.
4. Acute pulmonary embolism, right lower lobe, confirmed by CT angiography.
5. Mild acute kidney injury, resolving, attributed to diuresis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient presented to the Emergency Department (ED) with three days of
progressive shortness of breath (SOB), orthopnea, and bilateral lower
extremity edema. The patient also reported intermittent chest pain (CP)
described as pressure-like, worse with exertion, without radiation.
Initial workup in the ED included chest x-ray, which showed pulmonary
vascular congestion consistent with CHF exacerbation, and no evidence of
pneumonia. Given the acute SOB and CP, a CT chest was obtained to
evaluate for possible pulmonary embolism; the CT chest showed a filling
defect in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery, and a subsequent CT
angiography study confirmed acute pulmonary embolism in that location.
The patient was
adrnitted to the general medicine service for further management, with a
cardiology consult obtained given the CHF exacerbation and new PE.

HOSPITAL COURSE
The patient was diuresed with intravenous furosemide over the first 48
hours, with a net negative fluid balance of approximately 6 liters and
significant improvement in dyspnea. Home blood pressure medications were
held on admission given borderline low blood pressures, then gradually
resumed and adjusted prior to discharge. An echocardiogram was completed
during this admission, showing a reduced ejection fraction of 35 percent,
down from a prior known ejection fraction of 45 percent one year ago. The
cardiology consult team recommended optimization of guideline-directed
heart failure therapy prior to discharge. Anticoagulation was started for
the newly confirmed pulmonary embolism, with a plan to continue for at
least three months and reassess at follow-up. Renal function was
monitored daily; the admission creatinine was mildly elevated at 1.6
mg/dL, improving to 1.4 mg/dL by the day of discharge, attributed to a
combination of diuresis and improved cardiac output rather than
intrinsic kidney disease. Blood glucose was monitored throughout the
admission and remained within the patient's usual range on the home DM2
regimen; no adjustment to diabetes medications was required. The patient
remained afebrile throughout admission with no evidence of active
infection. A colonoscopy had been recommended by the patient's primary
care physician prior to this admission and was not performed during this
stay; it has been scheduled for 2026-08-15 as an outpatient procedure. By
hospital day four the patient was ambulating without difficulty,
saturating well on room air, and tolerating a low-sodium diet without
symptoms, and was deemed appropriate for discharge home with services.

PROCEDURES THIS ADMISSION
1. Transthoracic echocardiogram, completed 2026-07-02, showing reduced
   ejection fraction of 35 percent.
2. CT angiography of the chest, completed 2026-07-02, confirming acute
   pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe.
3. Outpatient colonoscopy, scheduled for 2026-08-15, not yet performed.

Take all medications exactly as prescribed. Do not resume any medication
that was stopped during this admission unless your primary care provider

RETURN PRECAUTIONS

Call 911 or go to the nearest Emergency Department (ED) right away if you
experience any of the following: chest pain (CP) that does not go away
with rest, severe shortness of breath (SOB) at rest, fainting, or
coughing up blood.

Call St. Anselm Medical Center's cardiology clinic during business hours
if you notice mild swelling in your legs that is new or getting worse, a
weight gain of more than three pounds in one day, or if you have
questions about your new blood thinner medication.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENTS

f/u with primary care physician in 1 week to recheck basic metabolic
panel and review the potassium result.
f/u with cardiology in 2 weeks to reassess heart failure symptoms and
review anticoagulation for the pulmonary embolism.
f/u with primary care physician in 3 months for routine DM2 and HTN
management.
Outpatient colonoscopy scheduled for 2026-08-15; you will receive
separate instructions for bowel preparation before that date.

DIET AND ACTIVITY

Continue a low-sodium diet, less than 2 grams of sodium per day. Weigh
yourself each morning at the same time and record the result. Call the
clinic if your weight increases by more than three pounds in a single
day or five pounds in a week. Gradually increase walking distance as
tolerated; avoid heavy lifting for two weeks.

MEDICATION SAFETY NOTE

Because you are now taking apixaban, a blood thinner, watch for unusual
bruising, bleeding gums, blood in your urine or stool, or a headache
that does not go away, and seek care promptly if any of these occur.

PATIENT EDUCATION

You were provided written and verbal education on heart failure
self-management, including daily weights, sodium restriction, and
recognizing early warning signs of fluid overload. You were also
counseled on the purpose, dosing, and bleeding precautions for your new
blood thinner, apixaban, and confirmed understanding by teach-back.

IMMUNIZATIONS AND SCREENING

Influenza vaccine status reviewed; up to date per patient report.
Pneumococcal vaccine status reviewed; recommend discussing with primary

Colon cancer screening addressed; outpatient colonoscopy already
